definition: A hardware feature (since NVIDIA Ampere) that splits one data-center GPU into up to seven isolated mini-GPUs, each with its own slice of memory and compute, so several small jobs can share a GPU without interfering.

Giving a job less than a whole GPU, by hardware partitioning (MIG), space sharing (MPS) or time-slicing. It raises utilization for small jobs such as notebooks and light inference, at some cost in isolation.
Letting several workloads take turns on one GPU. Cheap and flexible, but with no memory or fault isolation: if one workload crashes, all sharing the GPU go down.
Placing the GPUs of a job according to the physical network: for example keeping a tensor-parallel group inside one NVLink domain or one rack, so its heavy traffic never crosses slower links.
Idle GPUs scattered across many servers or racks in pieces too small for the next job. The cluster looks partly free, yet a large job cannot start.
A placement policy that fills one server or rack before using the next, keeping whole units free for large jobs. The opposite, spread placement, improves resilience but fragments capacity.
The share of installed GPUs assigned to some job at a given moment. It says nothing about whether the assigned GPUs are busy; it is the first and loosest utilization measure.
How busy the GPU's streaming multiprocessors actually are, as measured by telemetry such as DCGM. A GPU can be allocated and report 100% 'utilization' in simple tools while its SMs are mostly idle.
The share of a training run's wall-clock time spent making progress, after time lost to failures, restarts and re-computing work since the last checkpoint. Meta reported over 90% for Llama 3.
Average time from a failure to the job running productively again: detection, isolating the bad node, restarting and re-doing work since the last checkpoint.
A scheduler stopping (and usually requeuing) a lower-priority job to give its GPUs to a higher-priority one. It lets clusters lend idle capacity without blocking urgent work.
A fair-share rule for clusters with several resources (GPUs, CPUs, memory): each team's share is judged by the resource it uses most of, so no team can starve others by hoarding one resource.
NVIDIA's open-source daemon and tools for monitoring and managing data-center GPUs: health checks, diagnostics, error alerts and power policies, exported to schedulers and Kubernetes.

NVIDIA's cluster-management software (from the 2022 Bright Computing acquisition) that provisions, configures and monitors the servers, OS images and schedulers of a GPU cluster; now part of Mission Control.
One GPU used (or rented) for one hour: the unit in which GPU clouds price capacity and in which utilization economics are measured.
NVIDIA's disclosed commitments to pay cloud providers for capacity over several years (used for DGX Cloud and its own research). They appear in its filings as purchase commitments, not as revenue.

An open-source Kubernetes API from NVIDIA's Dynamo project that describes a whole multi-component inference system as one resource and schedules it with hierarchical gang and topology-aware placement.
